summary: Flame in Freefall is a platform we developed for the NASA 2026 Hackathon to make research on combustion in microgravity easier to explore and understand. Our project consists of three main sections. The first is dedicated to BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) experiments, where users can search for and explore detailed information about different experiments and their findings. The second provides a similar experience for FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment), allowing users to explore its experiments and related research. The third section is an AI-powered chatbot where users can enter their own API key and interact with an AI assistant. They can ask questions and learn about various aspects of combustion in freefall, including flame behaviour and fire safety in microgravity. Our goal is to bring experimental research and AI-powered assistance together in one place, making NASA's microgravity combustion research more accessible, interactive, and easier to understand.
details:
Flame.AI – Making Space Combustion Research More Accessible

Flame.AI is a research platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the challenge Flame in Freefall. The idea behind our project is simple: make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to explore, understand, and learn from by bringing experimental data and AI-powered assistance together in one place.

Our platform has three main sections, each designed to serve a different purpose.

1. BASS Explorer

This section focuses on NASA's Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiments. It allows users to explore 129 experimental records through searchable data, interactive filters, graphs, and detailed experiment information. Users can investigate how different factors influence the burning and suppression of solid materials.

2. FLEX Explorer

The second section is dedicated to NASA's Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experiments. It contains 274 experimental records and provides similar features for exploring liquid-fuel combustion. Users can examine experimental results, visualize data, and compare different parameters to better understand how flames behave and eventually extinguish in microgravity.

3. Flame.AI Assistant

We also wanted to make scientific information easier to understand, so we developed an AI-powered chatbot using the Google Gemini API. Users can enter their own API key and ask questions related to microgravity combustion, NASA's BASS and FLEX experiments, flame behaviour, ignition, extinction, and fire safety in space. This makes the platform more interactive and gives users a way to explore concepts beyond the available datasets.

Benefits and Intended Impact

One of the biggest challenges with scientific research is that experimental data can be difficult to navigate and interpret, especially for people who are new to the subject. Flame.AI aims to address this by organizing complex information into an interactive and user-friendly platform.

Instead of going through large amounts of raw data manually, users can search for specific experiments, apply filters, visualize results, and use the AI assistant to clarify their doubts. We hope this will make microgravity combustion research more approachable for students, educators, and researchers.

The larger goal is to contribute to a better understanding of how fire behaves in space. This is particularly important for spacecraft and future space habitats, where fire safety is a major concern. The knowledge gained from such research can help support the development of safer environments for astronauts on long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars.

Tools and Technologies Used

We used Python as the primary programming language for developing the application and handling the experimental data. Pandas was used for organizing, processing, and filtering the BASS and FLEX datasets. Interactive visualization tools were incorporated to help users explore experimental results through graphs and comparisons. We also integrated the Google Gemini API to power the AI chatbot.

The platform is designed to be accessible through a web browser and does not require any specialized hardware. The chatbot follows a Bring Your Own API Key approach, allowing users to connect their own Gemini API key.

Creativity and Innovation

What makes Flame.AI different is the way it brings multiple research tools together instead of treating them as separate resources. We didn't want to build just another chatbot or a website that displays experimental data. We wanted to create a platform where users could actually interact with NASA's combustion experiments, explore the results, identify patterns, and get explanations whenever they needed them.

Combining NASA's BASS and FLEX datasets with interactive visualization and AI assistance makes the platform useful for both exploring existing research and learning about the science behind it.

Factors Considered During Development

While developing Flame.AI, we focused on making the platform easy to use, accessible, and useful for people with different levels of scientific knowledge. We considered how students might use it to learn about combustion, how researchers might use it to explore experimental records, and how others interested in space science could use the AI assistant to understand unfamiliar concepts.

We also wanted to keep the platform accessible without subscriptions or paid access tiers. The user-provided API key approach helps us avoid depending on a shared, project-funded AI subscription.

Through Flame.AI, our aim is to make complex scientific research easier to explore and understand. We hope our project can help more people engage with microgravity combustion research and appreciate why understanding fire in space is so important for the future of human space exploration.
